extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (elementary/secondary schools and postsecondary institutions), Title IX Coordinators, school administrators, compliance officers
extracted.subtask_short: Title IX compliance for education recipients
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance and standards for how educational institutions must define actual knowledge, designate and authorize Title IX Coordinators, receive reports of sexual harassment, and respond (including K–12-specific rules). Covers notification, training, supportive measures, formal complaints, and related procedural obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation and authorization of a Title IX Coordinator (§106.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must designate “at least one” employee to serve as a Title IX Coordinator and must also “authorize” the Title IX Coordinator to meet specific responsibilities and to coordinate the recipient's overall efforts to comply with Title IX and these final regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should ensure the Title IX Coordinator has sufficient authority to perform duties. The Department recognizes recipients may designate multiple Title IX Coordinators or deputy coordinators if necessary, but will not require multiple coordinators; authorization (not merely designation) is required so the coordinator can fulfill obligations under the regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator contact information and public notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must notify their educational community of the contact information for the Title IX Coordinator and post that contact information prominently on the recipient's website and in handbooks or catalogs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact information must include an office address, telephone number, and electronic mail address. Recipients must expressly state that “any person” may report sexual harassment at any time (including during non-business hours) using the listed telephone number, email, or mail to the office address. Posting aims to provide clear, accessible reporting channels and to emphasize that giving notice does not require an in-person appointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of actual knowledge — employee training/reporting obligations do not alone create authority (§106.30)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere ability or obligation to inform a student about how to report sexual harassment or having been trained to do so will not qualify an individual as one who has authority to institute corrective measures on behalf of the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may train many employees or impose mandatory reporting without those employees becoming officials with authority solely by virtue of training or reporting obligations; the Department will hold the recipient accountable for meeting response obligations but not for designating every trained reporter as an official with authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual knowledge in elementary and secondary schools — notice to any employee triggers response
rubrics_metrics.description: For elementary and secondary schools, notice of sexual harassment to any employee of the school constitutes actual knowledge to the recipient and triggers the recipient's obligation to respond to sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes principals, teachers, school counselors, coaches, school bus drivers, paraeducators, and all other employees. This expansion is intended because young children may not seek out specific employees to disclose misconduct; it arguably broadens school obligations compared to prior guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual knowledge in postsecondary institutions — notice to Title IX Coordinator or officials with authority
rubrics_metrics.description: For postsecondary institutions, actual knowledge is conveyed by notice to the Title IX Coordinator or to officials with authority to institute corrective measures on behalf of the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postsecondary institutions retain discretion over how other employees respond and may train employees without automatically making them officials with authority; this approach respects postsecondary autonomy and student choices about disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may receive notice and how notice may be conveyed
rubrics_metrics.description: A Title IX Coordinator, an official with authority, and any employee of an elementary and secondary school may receive notice through an oral report, a written report, personal observation, a newspaper article, an anonymous report, or various other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imputation of knowledge based solely on vicarious liability or constructive notice is insufficient to constitute actual knowledge. Recipients cannot ignore sexual harassment if they have actual knowledge via any of these channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients' obligation to promptly offer supportive measures (§106.44(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recipient has actual knowledge of sexual harassment, the recipient must promptly offer supportive measures to a complainant and inform the complainant about how to file a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures must be offered irrespective of whether the complainant files a formal complaint; documenting offers and measures may help recipients demonstrate they were not deliberately indifferent and may reduce litigation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may designate officials with authority to institute corrective measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may, at their discretion, expressly designate specific employees as officials with authority to institute corrective measures on behalf of the recipient, and may inform students of such designations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a person is an official with authority is fact-specific and the Department will look to federal case law applying the Gebser/Davis framework. Providing a list of such officials can increase clarity for students and employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: K–12 third-party reporting rights and parental/guardian representation (§106.6(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties (e.g., parents, guardians, friends, trusted adults) have the right to report sexual harassment to the school's Title IX Coordinator, and parents/guardians have legal rights to act on behalf of a complainant (or respondent) in any Title IX matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a complainant tells a third party who reports the misconduct, the school is charged with actual knowledge and must promptly respond, even if the third party has no affiliation with the school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputation of knowledge limitations — respondent-only knowledge does not trigger actual knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual knowledge requirement is not satisfied when the only official or employee of the recipient with actual knowledge of the harassment is the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the only person aware is the respondent, the recipient may not have the opportunity to respond; but if the complainant tells another school employee then the school's obligations are triggered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of training materials (§106.45(b)(10)(i)(D))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations require recipients to publish training materials on recipient websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to prescribe particular training techniques beyond statutory/regulatory requirements but requires transparency by making training materials publicly accessible; recipients retain flexibility in how they meet training requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients' discretion to train or require reporting without expanded liability
rubrics_metrics.description: A postsecondary institution may train or require all employees to report sexual harassment or to inform students about how to report without fearing the Department will treat those employees as officials with authority simply because of training or reporting obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability under the regs depends on actual notice to a Title IX Coordinator or official with authority, not on broad institutional training practices alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to clearly state reporting options and hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must state that any person may report sexual harassment using the listed contact information for the Title IX Coordinator and specify that such reports may be made at any time (including during non-business hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision aims to remove barriers (like needing an in-person appointment) and to provide accessible reporting mechanisms including phone, email, or mail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal complaint filing methods and Title IX Coordinator's role
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations revise the definition of “formal complaint” to specify that a formal complaint may be filed in person, by mail, or by email using the listed contact information for the Title IX Coordinator; the Title IX Coordinator retains discretion to sign a formal complaint and is not a complainant or party when doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the recipient's ability to initiate the §106.45 grievance process when safety or other concerns require investigation even if the complainant does not file, while keeping the Title IX Coordinator neutral as not being a party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification duties about non-discrimination and reporting procedures (§106.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.8, recipients must notify students and employees of the recipient's policy of non-discrimination under Title IX, the Title IX Coordinator's contact information, and information about how to report and file complaints of sex discrimination and formal complaints of sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should disseminate these notices broadly so all community members know how to report and where to obtain supportive measures and information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and administrative burdens for large recipients
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory obligations (such as designation of a Title IX Coordinator) apply to each recipient regardless of enrollment size or number of campuses; recipients may designate multiple coordinators or deputies as needed but are not mandated to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must balance administrative burdens with Title IX obligations; the Department expects recipients to take administrative steps (e.g., multiple coordinators) when necessary to meet obligations effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department accountability expectations for Title IX Coordinator training and impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will hold the recipient accountable for having a Title IX Coordinator who has been trained to serve free from bias, impartial, and trained with materials that do not rely on sex stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should ensure training materials and selection/authorization of coordinators promote impartiality and avoid bias; failure to do so may affect Department enforcement assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational ombudspersons and confidential resources — fact-specific confidentiality status
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an organizational ombudsperson or similar campus confidential resource is an “official with authority to institute corrective measures” requires a fact-specific inquiry; the Department encourages recipients to examine how such resources operate within their systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For elementary and secondary schools, notice to any employee (including an ombudsperson) triggers response obligations; for postsecondary institutions, recipients should clarify whether ombudspersons are confidential to ensure parties understand which conversations remain confidential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on construing reporting obligations to create widespread authority
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employee's mere ability or obligation to report up the supervisory chain were sufficient to qualify that employee as an official with authority, then virtually every employee might be deemed an official — the final regulations therefore distinguish these concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final sentence in §106.30 clarifies that reporting obligations or training do not alone confer authority; the Department uses this distinction to preserve the purpose of the Gebser/Davis actual knowledge framework in administrative enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient-level legal effect and interaction with State laws and other guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: These final regulations apply at the Federal level; State laws may exceed these requirements but must not conflict. The Department acknowledges State mandatory reporter laws and notes recipients should ensure compliance without assuming Federal rules displace non-conflicting State obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients in states with more expansive mandatory reporter statutes should follow State requirements where applicable; the Department's expansion for elementary/secondary schools aligns with many State laws but does not require alignment beyond non-conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accessibility of reporting channels to reduce barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: By requiring posting of coordinator contact information (phone, email, address), clarification that any person may report at any time, and the ability to file formal complaints by multiple methods, the regulations aim to ensure students and employees have clear, accessible reporting channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessible reporting (including non-business hours and electronic methods) is intended to increase the likelihood of reporting and timely responsive measures; recipients should implement website and handbook postings and communication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department's reliance on federal case law (Gebser/Davis) to determine officials with authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a person constitutes an official with authority to institute corrective measures is a fact-specific determination and the Department will look to federal case law applying the Gebser/Davis framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may designate officials with authority but should be mindful that courts assess authority factually; documenting designations and authorities can promote clarity and reduce dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient burden is to ensure clear channels and trained coordinator, not to expand liability via training choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations place the burden on the recipient to designate and authorize a Title IX Coordinator, to provide contact information, and to ensure the coordinator is trained and impartial; they do not penalize recipients for choosing to train many employees or require reporting where the recipient does not designate those employees as officials with authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients retain discretion in training and reporting policies; they should balance institutional needs with the regulatory requirement that actual knowledge requires notice to the coordinator or officials with authority (except K–12 where any employee triggers actual knowledge).
